q: You want help from an experienced operator you've never met. Which first message is most likely to get a useful reply?
options: 'Would you be my mentor? I've followed your work for years and would really love to learn from you.'
'Could I ask you two questions about how you priced your first contracts, in a 15-minute call?'
'Can I pick your brain over coffee some time? I'm flexible on dates and happy to travel.'
A long message with your full pitch deck attached, so they have all the context up front.
why: A small, specific, time-limited ask is easy to say yes to and shows why you chose that person. Mentorship usually grows out of a few good exchanges like this, not out of asking for the title.

q: A mentor suggested a change to your pricing a month ago. What is most likely to make them want to keep helping you?
options: Telling them what you tried and what happened, even though it didn't fully work
Agreeing with everything they said in the call so they feel properly listened to
Offering them a small amount of equity as a thank-you for that one conversation
Waiting until you have a major success to share before getting back in touch
why: Closing the loop shows follow-through and lets them see that their help made a difference. That is often what turns a one-off conversation into an ongoing relationship.

q: A mentor has helped you three times. When does it generally make sense to offer them a formal advisor role?
options: Straight away, as a thank-you for the three times they've already helped you for free
When their well-known name would look impressive on your website and in your investor slides
Never, because advisors should only ever be paid in cash, never with company equity
When you need ongoing help in one area, they've delivered before and you can agree terms
why: An advisor role is a defined commitment, usually with equity attached, so it fits an ongoing, specific need and someone who has proven reliable. A written agreement, reviewed by a lawyer, sets out what each side expects.

q: An advisor's equity vests monthly over two years with a three-month cliff. They stop helping after two months. What generally happens to their grant?
options: They keep the whole grant, because it was promised to them at the start
They keep two months' worth of the grant, because vesting is monthly
Nothing has vested yet, so they generally receive none of the grant
They keep half the grant, because they completed most of the cliff
why: Nothing vests before the cliff is reached, so leaving at two months generally means no equity. The exact outcome depends on the written agreement, which a lawyer should review.

q: Your number of active users fell this month. What should your monthly update do?
options: Leave that metric out this month and bring it back once it has recovered
Report it as a lowlight, with the likely cause and what you're doing about it
Replace it with a different metric that went up, so the update stays positive
Skip this month's update and send a double-length update when the numbers improve
why: Updates build trust because they are consistent and honest. Readers notice when a number disappears, and seeing how you handle a bad month tells them more than a good month does.
